title: Quant research resources
tagline: From one backtest to a research process: the papers, the data, and the tape they get re-run on.
intro: A curated list for learning systematic investing research, ordered the way the work happens: the data you test on, what makes a backtest number mean something, the factors and events the literature found, what it costs to trade them, and the markets beyond stocks.

The core list uses the paper that introduced the effect, the official documentation, or the repository that implements it. Where the terminal can re-run a paper, the entry names the data the re-run uses and links to the library study and to RUN IT. Stock re-runs use the US tape (companies that later delisted are in it from 1998, survivors only before) and fundamentals by filing date, which are thin before about 1998 (re-runs start in 1990 at the earliest); the others run on the S&P 500 index, resolved Polymarket markets or Binance pairs. Each re-run approximates the paper rather than repeating it, and the terminal prints the approximation note with every run: what it holds, over what data, and where it departs from the original. RUN IT shows the finding as DATA VALIDATED, TRADE-OFF or NO EDGE, gross of costs, and says so on every output. Where the library carries the paper but has no runnable spec for it yet, the entry links to the library entry alone.
Read Start here first. After that, use it as a reference.

sections.title: Start here: the minimum mental model
sections.blurb: Read these in order if you are new to the field. The practical companion is the learn path: Become a quant and The findings system.

sections.title: 1. Data: the tape you test on
sections.blurb: Most bad backtests are bad data. A universe without the dead, fundamentals seen before they were filed, and prices without corporate actions each add returns that never existed.

sections.title: 2. The backtest: what makes a number mean something
sections.blurb: Multiple testing, overfitting, decay after publication, and how to run an event study. This section is why the terminal reports a deflated Sharpe and a walk-forward split on every run.

sections.title: 3. Factors and anomalies
sections.blurb: The cross-section: value, momentum, quality, low risk, size, reversal. Every entry links the original paper, the library study where there is one, and RUN IT where the terminal re-runs it on US stocks.

sections.title: 4. Events, flows and seasonality
sections.blurb: What happens after earnings, buybacks, dividends, index changes and insider trades, and the calendar effects that refuse to die.

sections.title: 5. Macro, rates and other asset classes
sections.blurb: The Fed, the curve, recessions, currencies, commodities and bonds.

sections.title: 6. Costs, execution and sizing
sections.blurb: Gross returns are the start of the conversation. These are the papers on what is left after trading, and how much to bet.

sections.title: 7. Alt markets: prediction markets, crypto, sports, memecoins
sections.blurb: Markets with their own literature and their own data problems. The memecoin graveyard has no paper yet because no free feed sells the dead; QuantGPT records them.

sections.title: 8. Machine learning in asset pricing
sections.blurb: Where the field is going, and the two papers to read before believing a model.

sections.title: 9. Tools and open data
sections.blurb: Official sources and open code. This list is the papers and the tape; awesome-quant is the code.

sections.title: Frontier and watchlist
sections.blurb: Kept apart from the core list because the evidence changes quickly. Verified on the date at the top.

policy: A core source must be one of the following: the paper that introduced the effect; the specification or official documentation that defines the data; the repository that implements it; or a replication that states its universe, window, survivorship treatment, costs and out-of-sample method.
Return claims need the universe, the window, the survivorship treatment, the cost assumption and the out-of-sample method. Otherwise the number is omitted.

Where an entry carries RUN IT, the terminal shows the finding (DATA VALIDATED, TRADE-OFF or NO EDGE) with the walk-forward split and a deflated Sharpe, gross of costs, and says so on every output. Nothing on this page is investment advice.
